references.text: The brothers react to Joseph's dream with even greater hatred and ask if he will really rule over them.
The brothers call Joseph 'the dreamer' and plan to kill him, as a direct result of the hatred the dreams caused.
Jacob dreams of a ladder reaching heaven, which shows the importance of dreams and God's communication through them in the lives of the patriarchs.
The cupbearer and the baker dream while in prison, and Joseph interprets their dreams—a continuation of the dream theme that began with his own dreams.
Pharaoh has dreams that Joseph interprets, leading to his elevation—an fulfillment of his youthful dreams.
Joseph remembers his dreams when his brothers bow down before him in Egypt, as a direct fulfillment of what he dreamed.
The psalm describes how Joseph was sent ahead to Egypt and tested by the Lord's word, a reference to his dreams and their fulfillment.
This verse illustrates the direct fulfillment of the dream mentioned in Gen 37:5, where hatred turns into submission as part of God's redemptive history.
This verse highlights the ironic tension between the brothers' hatred (Gen 37:5) and their lack of insight into Joseph's true identity and role.
This verse establishes a clear theological parallel in which jealousy toward the youngest brother (who receives God's plan) is a recurring theme in the history of the patriarchs.
This verse shows the theological completion of the conflict started in Gen 37:5, where hatred is replaced by acknowledgment of sin and a plea for reconciliation.
